item.title: Chas Freeman: Israel-Turkey Conflict Could Explode Into War
item.description:
Ambassador Chas Freeman was a former Assistant Secretary of Defense, earning the highest public service awards of the Department of Defense for his roles in designing a NATO-centred post-Cold War European security system and in reestablishing defence and military relations with China. He served as U. S. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia during operations Desert Shield and Desert Storm.

Welcome back. We are joined today by Ambassador Chas Freeman, uh the former US Ambassador to Saudi Arabia and also uh the former Assistant Secretary of uh Defense. Uh thank you for coming back on uh the show. >> Very glad to be with you, Glenn. >> Um we knew for a long time that uh well, the the relationship between uh Turkey and Israel was uh a difficult one. Indeed, uh uh we see this has become much worse uh in this struggle over well, post-Assad Syria. Indeed, all

those years of uh this uh war against Syria, we saw you had this grand coalition between the US, the Gulf states, Turkey, Israel, various, you know, jihadist groups uh all, you know, with a common go- common goal of toppling Assad, but uh uh I guess a lot of this uh coalition well, would predictably fall apart after Assad would be gone and the common interest would be gone and I guess the main two contenders for influence in uh post-Assad Syria would be Turkey and Israel.

And uh now we see that the Israel attacked uh this airbase in Syria, the Abu al-uh Dhuhur uh airbase and uh we are told, although the I don't think Turkey has confirmed it yet, that they either had troops there or they planned to send troops. Anyways, uh it seems that uh yeah, the the rivalry over influence in uh Syria is now sparking or intensifying a conflict between Israel and Turkey that uh well, could potentially, at least, escalate uh

to something like a war. And indeed, if you listen to some of the rhetoric from people like uh Naftali Bennett, uh Turkey seems more of a threat to Israel than even Iran. So, it um yeah, I was I I wanted to get uh your view on this, how you the situation and uh also the recent developments. >> Well, I think it's very complicated as everything in that region seems to be. Um I think uh the the state of US-Turkish relations is also a factor

in this. Um Uh and I'll come to that. Uh but basically uh one of the major strategic achievements uh of Israel um in in the region uh in its view uh was the disarmament and subjugation of Syria. Uh subordination to Israeli control. Uh that is not just the seizure of some territory in in Syria which Israel clearly plans to keep, but um uh the uh the removal of uh what Israel Katz, the um

uh Israeli defense minister, described as a hostile force on Israel's borders. Of course, there's a certain irony there because Israel has no borders. Uh it simply expands them wherever it wishes. And then it's surprised that the people it has dislodged uh have an opinion against it. Anyway, um the uh there is a contest going on in Syria between uh the Turks and Israelis. The Turks have just supplied according to Israeli sources um supplied Syria with uh military

equipment including tanks which would give it some minimal ability to resist uh the Israeli incursions. I don't believe there were Turkish troops at that airbase. I think they've clearly said there weren't. Um whether they, you know, of course, one has to take denials from governments with a grain of salt. In fact, the usual rule is you should never believe anything until it's been officially denied. Uh but um uh in any event um uh this is a real contest and it's just been complicated by

the Syrian foreign minister uh declaring that Syria is in the is considering whether it should join the Pakistani, Saudi, Turkish entente. Um which one function of which clearly perhaps the principal function of which is uh to counter Israel. Uh and um so um this is I think a clever diplomatic move. There's no indication that Syria would actually be welcomed into that entente. Uh um but um

there it is. There's also a Syrian statement uh that um they might be open to a Pakistani brokered uh rapprochement with Iran. And what this illustrates uh >> [snorts] >> is what we've talked about before. And that is the displacement of ideology and theology as guiding forces for the foreign policies of countries in this region and in ja- in fact generally. Uh they're now guided by national interests. Uh and the Shia

uh Sunni split which was a de- defining uh chasm in the affairs of the region earlier uh is now far less important. Um Turkey obviously is Sunni. Uh with regard to the Turkish uh Israeli relationship there are several elements worth thinking about. Um one is uh of course that uh the last poll I saw uh showed that 97% of Turks um were against Israel. Why? I mean, the Israelis have killed Turks who were attempting to aid

Palestinians in Gaza with um humanitarian assistance. Uh and as you indicated uh the rhetoric from Naftali Bennett and others in in Israel now is um uh equates Turkey with Iran as a potential enemy of the existence of Israel. Which maybe it is. Um anyway, um so there is that. Then there is the question of the F-35, which uh President Erdoğan wants to acquire and which Donald Trump

appears inclined to release to him. Uh Israel is going hammer and tongs in the United States against such a transaction on the grounds that it would uh impair the so-called qualitative edge that the Israelis enjoy as a matter of law in the United States. Um uh that is American underwriting of military superiority for Israel in West Asia. Uh so that's a factor. Uh and lurking behind all of this is the the continued um

American neglect of relations with Turkey um going back to previous administrations, not really repaired by the bromance between Trump and Erdoğan. Um And the fact that Turkey is uh uh an essential partner or at least um uh an essential um uh non-partner in uh or non-antagonist in a wide variety of American and European interests. Um

you simply can't conduct a policy toward Syria, Israel, Palestine, Iraq, Iran, um uh Greece, Cyprus, the Eastern Mediterranean, the Balkans, Black Sea, the Caucasus, the Central Asian region including Afghanistan, um the Persian Gulf region, um uh and uh the European Union or NATO uh and Russia uh without uh Turkish uh agreement or acquiescence. Uh so, um uh Israel sees Turkey

uh as a rival not just in the region, but in and in a rival for American affection or attention, uh given the level of interest that's involved, and the widening realization in the United States that Israel is not a strategic asset for America, but a strategic liability. So, this is a dangerous situation, and if indeed Syria is the prospective partner in the tripartite entente between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey, then uh I think we've got a game changer in the

region. Uh and and let me just uh finish [snorts] by saying, of course, that tripartite entente, uh whatever else it is, is a declaration by uh the major countries in the region uh of independence from reliance on American backing and support, which they no longer consider reliable. So, now they believe they must acquire self-reliance. This will involve re-diver- further diversifying their international relationships away from America, but more importantly, building

capabilities collectively and developing a habit of consultation on regional security affairs. Um this is obviously designed as a counter to Israel, which they see correctly as the principal source of instability in their region, uh a state that has no borders and that is expansionist, and which has aspirations for still greater domination of the region. Um and um uh so, um but the open question is, what relationship will this entente develop

with Iran? And I think it's entirely plausible, putting together the two Syrian statements, uh Pakistan perhaps mediating a uh a rapprochement between Syria and Ira- Iraq is sorry Ir- Iran. Um uh and uh the Iraqis developing a a slowly improving relationship with Syria, which is quite contrary to historical uh precedents. Uh this driven by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iraqi requirement to send oil out to the

Mediterranean through Syria, uh but also uh by the eclipse of uh theology as uh the driving force in the relations between the two. Uh Syria now under Salafi Islamic uh Sunni uh uh rule uh Iraq under Shia rule um and uh and and I think um uh all of this comes together um uh the question is what will the relationship between the tripartite um uh alliance or entente more accurately,

I think um uh and Iran be. And I can foresee a consultative relationship, not a membership in the in the entente, uh but something like the consultative relationship with Egypt that the other three parties had in dealing with regional efforts, regional ac- uh activities and developments. In other words, um a coordination mechanism, uh not a membership, uh maybe a dialogue partner relationship uh to use the ASEAN term.

So, I think this is what is happening between Turkey and Turkey and and Israel is really very important and a bit dangerous because Turkey is a formidable military power and um uh uh the Israelis who aspire to dominate the entire region uh have little hope of dominating Turkey. >> And just a quick thought on the possibility of Syria and Iran improving relations, that would be quite interesting. Uh last time we spoke, you also mentioned that

uh the Saudis could move a bit away from this uh you know, religious thinking and lean more into national interest and uh and uh it it reminds me a little bit about the 30 year war we had in Europe uh 500 years ago. That is when you saw Catholic France allying with the Protestant Swedes to balance off the again, the the Catholic Habsburgs. So, to avoid encirclement or the dominance >> But I think there is a parallel and and indeed the Saudis have moved well away from

religiously driven foreign policy. Um uh they're very much pursuing their national interest as they see it. Uh sometimes ineptly, of course. Um with this uh re-igniting of war with Ansar Allah, the Houthis in Yemen standing out as the prime example of uh foolish uh um and perhaps backing, perhaps not a direct action by the Saudis, uh but uh a collusive action with the government in Yemen, in South Yemen that they recognize.

Uh so, yeah, that is indeed uh uh a parallel and let me draw a further parallel because I think um if you could go back and look at uh the Peace of Westphalia, um which resulted from that uh confused contest, um uh people found uh a way of transcending religious differences uh in and creating uh uh a new state system in Europe. Uh and I think this is entirely possible within the Islamic context.

Uh that is to say, there is an Islamic law of statecraft, which is very rich, 1,500 years of it. Um and uh many principles in common between Shia and Sunni. Uh of course Shiism is uh and Sunni Islam are both internally divided, but but they have common principles um which uh people found it in the peace of Westphalia in Europe, and it could happen uh in the Gulf as well. One thing here

is that Israel has succeeded especially with the latest comments by Itamar Ben-Gvir, the uh Minister of Security in Israel uh advocating the murder of 50-60 Palestinians a day just as a matter of principle in Gaza. Um revealing himself to be not just a sadist we knew who he was, but uh but a mass murderer um with no humanity at all um this has united the 57 uh Muslim-dominated countries in the world behind

behind an anti-Israel policy, which is yet to be fully realized organizationally, but which is out there as a as a potential that the uh Israel and its friends should be worried about. >> Yeah. Well, um but on the religious line, it's quite [clears throat] interesting that the Russians were there for so long helping Assad to fight the well, essentially Julani and his crew, and then now we see Russia essentially well, seemingly being allowed to keep its military something that annoys the Europeans. I think that

was a I don't think, I know that was a key motivation for supporting the toppling of Assad as well to not just disentangle Syria from Iran, but also disentangle it from from Russia. Um but I uh I was wondering though, what do you think might be the the reactions here? Because again, if Israel uh wants to deter Turkey from uh from estab- establishing a base in Syria if that's indeed what they were intending to do. I assume that the Turks won't just pack up and leave and go

home. How do you think they're responding? Will they strengthen their own presence in Syria? Will they just send a lot of arms? How how might they respond? As you know, there's a possibility now Turkey and Israel going up the escalation ladder. I stress possibility not certainly of course. >> at the moment they're shadow boxing. They're not actually landing punches. Um but that could happen. Uh I think history teaches an important lesson

and that is don't mess with the Turks. Um I think you you you do that at your peril. Uh and uh so the Israelis are right to be concerned that they have a formidable opponent uh in Syria. Uh the Russian um presence in Syria is indeed another indicator of as you suggest of the eclipse of ideology or theology as a driving force in in foreign policy in this case uh in the foreign policy of Syria.

And I note that the Russians uh uh retain who uh retain an ability a diplomatic ability even though they are distracted at the moment by uh the war in Eastern Europe. Um they retain uh a diplomatic capability uh to mediate, to intervene, to broker um various arrangements between uh Turks and Israelis if that's possible. Um between Syrians and Iranians have uh and um

uh the United States uh and Western Europeans don't have that uh ability because we have cut off our uh dialogue with uh uh with Iran and Israel is now at odds with us across the board defiant on virtually every front determined to finish the extermination of Palestinians in Gaza to drive Palestinians out of the West Bank to annex Southern Lebanon to keep the territory it's taken in Syria

and to attack at will its neighbors um whenever they defy it so this is this is the source of instability in the region as I mentioned and and the appetite for instability in the region by Europeans and Americans is running quite low. >> Yeah by the way the the Russians I speak with they they argue now that it's not so bad actually that Assad is gone because it put an end to Russia's military participation but also

standing so close with Assad it it it created a lot of tensions between Russia and the Gulf states now that they they kind of divorced themselves from this it's it's easier to work with with the Gulf states and so it's it's interesting how you how things turn out but what else is there doing this relationship between the Turks and the Israelis and I just would add I think this is problematic for the Israelis I can understand why they might be concerned that Turkey has a massive conventional

army yeah huge population again and as you said the rivalry for US affection if you will that is you know they're NATO member Americans have nuclear weapons there it's it's it it is a problem but but you also see Erdogan he's seen his rhetoric seems to that the Israeli actions in the region it's now affecting Turkish security. So, how is an actual security competition or is

there is it more or is it more limited to Syria here? >> No, I think it's a broad broad-based uh competition in on all the fronts you mentioned um you've inadvertently reminded me of uh uh my chairmanship of the uh US-Turkish joint uh commission on military cooperation uh which took me to Ankara uh where I um uh one of the issues at the time was the Turks were attempting to procure uh tanker aircraft from the United States. Uh and the Israelis working through the

Greek lobby in the United States were trying very hard to snatch that contract away uh for the for and I was present at a discussion between our military representative in Ankara Major General Philip Newbold uh and the head of the Turkish Air Force General Burhan uh in which um General Burhan um uh in the congenial manner of the of the German of sorry the Turkish General Staff generally um said to Phil Newbold uh

"Phil, if you don't get me those aircraft, I'm going to get you into an I'm going to put you in a Turkish jail." And he said, "Have you ever seen a Turkish jail?" And Phil said, "No." And new and uh General Burhan said, "Well, did you see Midnight Express?" And Phil said, "Yes." And and um General Burhan said, "They exaggerated the amenities." So, the Turks don't play around, you know, anything. Anyway, um uh in the end they did get the aircraft uh and they used the tankers very effectively to send F-16s uh to

Libya uh against American wishes. Um, and um um, so everybody in the region is behaving quite independently. Uh, nobody regards the United States as reliable. Uh, and that includes Israel, of course. Um, which as I mentioned is now at odds with the United States across the board. This isn't going to go away if there is a new leader elected in Israel or or if uh, Prime Minister Netanyahu is reelected somehow. Um,

it's it's structural. Uh, and uh, everybody in the region is reacting to this. Um, I think believing that uh, Israel is now vulnerable and perhaps the Turks are motivated in part by that. >> How stable do you see I mean, if I would assess Turkey in the region, how I wouldn't just look at its interest. I would look at its um, I guess predictability and its path forward because what what I find interesting about Turkey is on one hand they they they do talk a lot about you know,

harmonizing interest with others in the region. Indeed last year I had a meeting in the Vatican with uh, uh, yeah, Jeffrey Sachs as well as the first lady of Turkey and you know, she was also stressing a lot how you need to have this you know, uh, bridging the differences between different religions and different uh, ethnic groups and you know, a lot of harmony in the language, but at the same time you also see in Turkish foreign policy they make deals and uh, you think you have an arrangement and then suddenly there's a knife in your back.

So, I'm just uh, well, especially with like for example, with the Russians they had a few instances as well. They as you know, for example, the Azov warrior from uh, which they they the Russians had apprehended, they were they were sent to Turkey. They weren't supposed to be sent back to Ukraine before after the war. The Turks just you know, went ahead and you know, and uh, same same as with the attack on Syria. The Russians thought they had an arrangement with the Turks, and uh you know, it didn't last very long. So, um my my impression of Turkey is yes, it's very independent actor. I think many countries like Russia prefers to look towards the Turks exactly

because they are they're able of acting independently, but at the same time they don't always seem um predictable or uh yeah, let's go trustworthy as well. >> Well, I think you raise a number of issues. It's been some years since I've been in Turkey, um but Turkish society has been uh divided between the secularism of the Kemalist element uh and the um Muslim Brotherhood orientation of the of Erdoğan and his followers. Um

and um of course, there was an alleged coup against um Erdoğan uh by supposedly led by um the Gülen movement, which has been ruthlessly repressed. Um and these these fissures exist in Turkish politics um with quite sharp differences between uh the uh the the the the followers of Atatürk and and uh and and the more Islamist uh democratic element uh uh behind Erdoğan.

Um and but in the middle of all this, let's not forget that the major national security issue that the Turks have faced internally, which was the uh violent opposition to terrorism of the uh PKK, the Kurdish Communist Party in in in uh in in Turkey, um uh has been has been uh set aside. Uh Abdullah Öcalan, who's the head of that party, um uh has made his peace with the Turkish government. Um PKK has basically uh

uh disarmed and um um uh the uh uh the Kurds over the border in uh in Syria also seem to be integrating slowly with the government in Damascus. Uh not focused uh so much on uh on uh uh uh opposition to Turkey and and uh in Kurdistan uh Iraqi Kurdistan um uh there's also um uh quite a move uh it seems toward um reconciliation with the Turks. So

so I I I think um it's a mixed picture. And the the erratic nature of Turkish policy uh reflects a strongman uh Erdogan who is now in charge. I mean, by comparison with Trump, he's steady and predictable as you can get, but um um uh most people would not apply that standard, I gather. Um uh and um uh so uh yes, there is the Turks again, one can't take them for granted and it's a mistake to do so.

Um but I think what Israel is doing um in Syria uh is and generally uh I refer back to the alienation of the 57 members of the Organization for Islamic Cooperation. Uh what they're doing is making an enemy of Turkey. Uh and I I know you and I have discussed before that um uh whereas Henry Kissinger remarked that even the paranoid have enemies, um uh I add the corollary that paranoid are particularly good at making enemies. Um and in this case, Israelis who are

very paranoid dominated by uh all sorts of um uh theories of global anti-Semitism and whatnot, uh uh which really don't hold up, but which guide their policy, um, they are making an enemy of Turkey. >> Yeah. No, no, I I agree. And well, also the the quote by Kissinger, I think is uh yeah, uh uh um yeah, a wise position to take because uh you know, yeah, the Israelis, as you

say, could be very um paranoid, but Turkey is a huge country, as I said before. It is has a formidable military force. And again, given that it could be a bit or proven in the past to be a bit unpredictable. And also, the region is shifting quickly. You don't know where the United States going to be standing in a year from now, especially after the defeat in Iran. And then you see Turkey making this, you know, defense pact with the with the Saudis and Pakistan. And I'm thinking this uh strategic uh shifting the strategic alignment uh uh very rapidly.

Yeah, what uh sorry. >> Yeah, yeah, I mean, no, I'm sorry. Uh I mean, you're absolutely correct. I mean, there is a parallel uh you're an expert on Russia. There's a parallel uh to what the Russians are doing, and that is giving up 300 years of effort to Europeanize themselves. Um and the Turks have done the same. Uh they now straddle uh the region. And don't forget uh the the list of uh uh uh Turkish uh uh influence on uh on other interests that I

mentioned. I mean, a vast number. I can't think of a country which is as important in the management of other relationships uh as as Turkey is. So, Turkey is really a fulcrum from, you know, which can leverage all kinds of things. Uh and it's a mistake not to pay attention to Turkey. Uh and maybe the Israelis have finally figured that out, but they're giving it the wrong kind of attention, in in my view, for their own long-term interests. >> I think what's happening with Yeah, I

like the way compare the Turkey to to Russia on this because it's hard to like overstate how much Europe is undergoing change. That is after the Cold War, the EU you know, aligned itself to hit more or less with the US well as it had been before, but the EU itself became a you know, always in literature conceptualized itself as a gravitational force. That is that the entire region all these neighbors kind of leaning in towards the EU. Everyone needs trade agreements. They're willing to accept the political conditions for trading

with the EU and essentially everyone is yeah, standing at the door asking what what they can do next and this was kind of the foundation of the regulatory power that Brussels enjoyed, but now the Russians have essentially said well this 300 years since Peter the Great of having a Western-centric foreign policy looking towards the Europeans for economic development, technology. This is over. We're going to look to the East and now you see the same from Turkey. And then even the Americans are now losing interest in in in Europe saying well, you're perhaps a third in our

priorities. This is this is new and with the end of this gravitational pull, the EU itself of course can begin to fragment because suddenly the collective bargaining power that created this gravitational pull. That was kind of the main incentive for transferring your sovereignty to Brussels. So anyways, I I get off bit off track here. What I want to do >> Well, I think I think it's very important. I mean the conceiving of European influence as a gravitational force is exactly the right

metaphor. It's been remarkably successful in extending its standards to the to its periphery and incorporating uh uh new members um uh who accept standards pioneered by uh Western Europeans. Um you know, this has been a great success story. What Europe has not been able to do is to cohere sufficiently to act beyond its immediate periphery. And it has in the case of the Ukraine war

acted so foolishly without any dialogue with Moscow, no effort to find a stable resolution of the security issues that Ukraine represents both for Russia and the rest of Europe. Um that um you know, it has um fouled its own nest, as it were. Um and uh there we are. Uh but at least you can count one blessing. I think Donald Trump just threatened to bomb Oman, an inoffensive neutral, diplomatically effective, and very helpful country um uh on the Arabian Peninsula facing the

Arabian Sea and Africa. Uh an imperial power in the past. Uh but so far as I know, he's not threatened to bomb Norway yet. Um presumably the save the whales people will try to persuade him to do that, but I don't know if Laura Loomer has yet been converted to their cause. >> I find it very strange this other people who are influencing Trump. It's uh deeply concerning to me, though. >> Well, Jacob, you've probably been, as I have

to the house of Rasputin in in the you know, but some of this is reminiscent of that. Uh Yeah. The last days of the Tsars. >> Uh no, it's uh yeah, fascinating who gets, you know, the the ear of the leaders. Uh But uh yeah, well, what I want to ask before I forgot, there was uh uh you know, let's say if from the Israeli perspective, it's uh there is good reasons to fear Turkey. Uh just I would like to make the point I do think they're unnecessarily making an enemy out of Turkey where it's not

necessary. Uh, I always make the point the same with Europeans and Russia. You have reasons to be concerned about the Russians, but making an enemy out of it must have been the Yeah, something for the history books in terms of stupidity. But if if we do recognize that Israel has some some legitimate concerns about Turkey, uh, what what can Israel really do? I mean, their weapon stockpiles have been depleted. Their military systems, their the personnel, I mean, they've been uh, largely exhausted. I think the head of the IDF warned that they were already profoundly overstretched. Uh, so, you

know, they're facing also they're already engaged in all these wars with Iran, Hamas, Hezbollah, Syria, Yemen. Uh, what What is the What What is the capacity now of the Israeli army to actually take on such a massive giant like Turkey? I mean, if you >> I don't think they have that capacity. I think a good deal of this is electoral rhetoric. Um, uh, talk You know, Israel, Israeli politics revolve around um, um,

declaring everybody to be an anti-semitic enemy. Um, and Turkey, you know, the 97% of Turks apparently um, are happy to accept that appellation. So, um, the uh, so part of it is that, but you know, but it is foolish because they don't have the capacity to do that. And they're doing this uh, it is possible to look at the past and to argue that um, one of the reasons that the Turks uh, had a diplomatic relationship with Israel and did trade with it and so on

was because uh, they had the Turks had an overwhelming desire to appease American interests which uh, were manipulated by Israel to its advantage. Uh, that's gone. Um, now the Turks still apparently facilitated the transport of oil through their territory uh, for the benefit of Israel. Um, uh, oil from Azerbaijan, I guess. Um, uh, but, um, uh, so, they're not, um, uh, actively

uh, acting against Israel, but then Israel isn't really actively acting against Turkey, either. I mean, this is a war that is being carried out by proxy uh, in uh, a war, um, a struggle uh, in Syria and in Kurdistan. Uh, Iraqi Kurdistan. Where the Israelis have entrenched themselves, as have the Americans. Uh, this is the reason that the Iranians have been bombing, uh, Iraqi Kurdistan, um, and, um, so, uh,

uh, you know, uh, the everything in the region operates independently, but it's all interconnected somehow. >> Yeah, that's, uh, good way of framing it. But, all be besides the material losses, though, and exhaustion in the Israel, there's also the the reputation it has. I mean, the reputation of Israel, I think, was quite important. I mean, on one hand, yes, the brutality they used against their enemies, it was, you know, or is always condemned because of the uh, yeah, the brutality of it. But, on

the other hand, this overwhelming superiority in force, it also established a powerful reputation for Israel that you would be careful before you go against it. Not only would you have a powerful Israel, but you would have powerful America standing behind it. But, the idea of reputation now seems to have been, uh, have suffered somewhat, and, uh, indeed, >> Well, I think it's been gravely tarnished. Um, and, you know, I mean, Israel basically has gotten by Israel is a, uh, a state established by Europeans European Jews.

Um and it has enjoyed honorary membership in Europe. Um you know, that's why it's in Eurovision and other things. Um And which is now controversial. Which never was before. I mean, Israelis uh are in West Asia, but they would prefer to be in Europe. And of course I I think it was a grave mistake not to uh allow uh European Jews to set up a state in Bavaria after World War but that is not what happened and um and uh we're left with

the results. But this uh European identity has worn thin. It's to the point of disappearing. I mean, no European would say anything like what Ben Gvir has just said. Uh no European would say anything like uh Bezalel uh Smotrich says. No European uh would dare um uh say the sorts of things that Netanyahu says uh about a seizure of territory by force and the eviction of the existing population and so forth. Uh your uh Israel is now a complete outlaw.

Uh it has departed from the norms of international law crafted by Europe. Uh it espouses no principles other than uh its own survival at the ex- whatever expense to others that entails. Uh it's lost the admiration of the West. Uh it never really had the admiration of the rest of the world. But now it has the opprobrium of the rest of the world and a rising percentage of people in the West who do not want to be associated with genocide, mass murder, torture, sodomy

in the prisons, and all the other ugly things that Israelis now uh stand for. So now when you talk about the IDF uh and if you were to say as Netanyahu used to claim that this was the world's most moral army, uh people would snicker. Um they would uh condemn you for moral blindness. Uh this is the world's most sadistic army. It is the most uncontrolled army. Uh it is the most brutal army. Uh and uh it is the most successful army

at making enemies for the state it serves uh that exists anywhere, despite some competition in um internationally. >> Yeah, and all it's not just reputation, I would say Israel itself has changed profoundly, at least since the '60s, '70s. I mean, the the kind of secular and uh yeah, different moral compass Israel had assumed to have back then, it's uh yeah, not recognizable compared to what they are today. And the

uh but this is also fueling in internal problems though, which is why I'm wondering well, there there's a lot a lot of consent on key issues like uh attacking Iran or uh you know, >> Lebanon. >> what they're doing in Gaza, Lebanon. They all the wars, that seems to be a unifier. But uh but beyond this, they have some profound problems at home though, some divisions which are hard to overcome. >> Well, some of those divisions um reflect the evolution of Zionism. Uh Zionism actually I mean, the initial uh

impetus for resettling uh European Jews in Palestine was actually a Christian invention. It wasn't a Jewish invention. Um and uh it was picked up later by secular Jews who you know, had Christmas trees in their living rooms and so forth. Um Hertzel um uh and uh and the initial uh impetus for the establishment of the state of Israel Zionism was it was basically modeled on Eastern European nationalism

that is ethnolinguistic self-determination. This case involving the transformation of religious communities into a presumed ethnicity. Which is of course I mean one of the great ironies is Golda Meir and others used to refer to the Palestinians as an invented people. But Israelis are an invented people. I mean they were Zionists are an invented people. Anyway Zionism has left Judaism far behind.

The Orthodox in in Israel the ultra-Orthodox the Haredim do not accept the existence of the Israeli state or the moral justification for it. And continue to practice a form of Judaism which has nothing to do with Zionism. They don't want to be associated with it. They're not prepared to defend it. They won't join the army if they can avoid it. And they devote themselves to religious studies. Secular Jews

have been squeezed out. There is now net immigration at quite a rate from Israel.
